notes:
I've drafted notes for each verse below. Most of the material comes from older commentaries collected on biblehub.com, studylight.org and blueletterbible.org, plus enduringword.com (Guzik) and preceptaustin.org. **What's missing:** my tool limits ran out before I could read anything from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org or the denominational sites (Ligonier, GTY, LCMS, Seedbed and others). So there's no Catholic, Orthodox, modern-scholarship or prosperity/hyper-grace section, and vv. 32, 36 and 45 are thin.

A note on the Enduring Word page: I read it in full, but it had no numbered sentences to cite, so those points just give the URL.

---

## Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 24:** Guzik says vv. 23–26 assume Israel has refused to be "reformed" by the earlier disasters, so God sends more. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-26/
- Barnes says "seven times" is the sabbatical number, used proverbially to remind the people of the covenant. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/26-42.html
- Barnes calls this section the fourth warning: God now sets Himself against a people who "will not be reformed". https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlv/leviticus/26-29.html

**v. 25:** Barnes says God will avenge the outraged cause of His covenant, by the sword, pestilence, famine, and captivity. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlv/leviticus/26-29.html

**v. 26:** Barnes: "to break the staff of bread" was a common saying for cutting off the bread supply, the staff of life. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlv/leviticus/26-29.html
- Guzik says ten women could share one oven because there was so little flour. He quotes Peter-Contesse that the bread would be weighed out in tiny portions (compare Ezekiel 4:16–17). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-26/

**vv. 27–28:** Keil & Delitzsch call this the fourth and severest stage. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/26-29.htm
- Guzik points out that even here God does not say He will abandon Israel, only that they will be cursed. He adds that these curses became the sad story of Israel's history. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-26/

**v. 29:** Benson says the curse was fulfilled, first in the siege of Samaria, 2 Kings 6:29; next in the siege of Jerusalem before the Babylonish captivity, Lamentations 4:10; and finally, in the last destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans. Gill retells Josephus' story of a woman named Mary during Titus' siege. Some Jewish writers think the curse also includes children eating their parents (Ezekiel 5:10). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/26-29.htm
- Calvin: the act would be unbelievable, but it shows how terrible it is to fall into the hands of God, when men, by adding crime to crime, cease not to provoke His wrath. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/26-29.html
- The Bible Hub study notes read the verse literally, then point to the cross: God spared not His "own Son" (Romans 8:32). https://biblehub.com/leviticus/26-29.htm

**v. 30:** Barnes: "high places" means raised sites used for false worship (Deuteronomy 12:2), apparently for Baal in particular. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/26-29.html
- Keil & Delitzsch: the word for idols literally means "clods," a scornful term. The idolaters' corpses would defile images that had themselves become "corpses" when they were smashed. "My soul shall abhor you" reflects God's holy nature, which must reject the sinner. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/26-29.htm
- Calvin: piling the idols together with the bones of the dead was as if the finger of God pointed out His abomination of their false worship. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/26-29.html
- Precept Austin notes a word pattern. The verb "abhor" appears five times in this chapter: God promises not to abhor Israel (vv. 11, 44), Israel abhors His laws (vv. 15, 43), and God abhors them for idolatry (v. 30). https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_26_commentary

**v. 31:** Matthew Henry thinks the "sanctuaries" are their synagogues where they met for religious worship. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_026.cfm

**v. 32:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls this prediction of a desolate land very remarkable, given that Assyrian conquerors usually sent settlers to farm and live in newly taken provinces. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/26-34.htm

**v. 33:** Guzik: Israel would be conquered, removed and scattered among the Gentiles. He notes that "scatter" is a farming word. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-26/

**vv. 34–35:**
- **Calvin:** God included the land in the Sabbath so that people would honour the Sabbath more. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/26-34.html
- **Benson:** the land gets the rest that the people through covetousness, would not give it. 2 Chronicles 36:21 gives this as a main reason for the 70-year captivity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/26-34.htm
- **Clarke** (citing Houbigant): about 490 years passed from Saul to the exile, which means 70 missed sabbath years, matching the 70-year captivity. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/26-34.html. Precept Austin follows the same 490-year reckoning. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_26_commentary
- **Matthew Henry:** the wording suggests the ground itself was pleased and easy when it was rid of the burden of such sinners (Romans 8:20). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_026.cfm
- **The commentators disagree on the arithmetic.** Clarke asks whether the sabbath-year law was kept until Saul's time. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/26-34.html. The Pulpit Commentary counts 863 years, in which one hundred and twenty-three sabbatical years should have been kept. https://biblehub.com/leviticus/26-34.htm. Coffman doubts that 53 were actually observed and suggests the round number of years (ten times seven) was considered as the fullness of judgment. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/26-34.html

**vv. 36–37:** Precept Austin, on "no strength to stand," calls the Nazi death camps a partial fulfillment of this horrible prophecy. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_26_commentary

**vv. 38–39:** Barnes: "iniquity" here means the punishment of their iniquity. He says Scripture does not make that trenchant division between sin and punishment which we are accustomed to do. Sin is its own punishment. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlv/leviticus/26-29.html

**v. 40:** Barnes: the Hebrew word for trespass means a wrong done to a person's rights, and here Yahweh treats the breaking of the covenant as a personal trespass. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/jps/leviticus/26-29.html
- A Bible Hub homily links this confession to Ezra 9, Nehemiah 1 and 9, and Daniel 9. https://biblehub.com/sermons/leviticus/26-42.htm

**v. 41:**
- **Ellicott:** an "uncircumcised heart" is perverse and stubborn, too proud to confess humbly (compare Acts 7:51). https://biblehub.com/leviticus/26-41.htm
- **Barnes:** they might keep the outward sign of the covenant, but the matching grace in the heart would be missing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/26-41.html
- **"Accept/make amends":** the Hebrew verb is the same one translated "enjoy" in v. 34. Ellicott: they will freely admit the punishment is less than they deserve. Keil & Delitzsch call the phrase a bold and paradoxical way of describing a complete change of heart. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/26-41.htm
- **Guzik:** they must recognise their sin and God's discipline, and accept that they were as bad as the Gentiles. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-26/
- **A Pulpit Commentary homily (Macdonald)** says they will confess in particular their capital sin in rejecting Christ. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/leviticus-26.html

**v. 42:**
- **Ellicott:** "remember" means to perform the covenant. Because "covenant" is repeated before each name, Jewish scholars of the Second Temple period concluded these were three separate covenants. The Aramaic Targums link them to Bethel, Moriah and the "pieces" of Genesis 15. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/26-42.htm
- **Gill:** the reversed order (Jacob to Abraham) has no satisfying explanation. The covenant chiefly concerns their descendants and the Messiah springing from them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/26-42.html
- **A Pulpit homily** on the reversed order: when the Jews humbly admit they are children of their recent sinful fathers, God will acknowledge them as the children of their earlier faithful ancestors. https://biblehub.com/sermons/leviticus/26-42.htm
- **Matthew Poole** on "remember the land": the land now seems to be forgotten, neglected and despised, as if God had never chosen it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/26-42.htm

**v. 43:** Barnes sets up a contrast: the land enjoys its sabbaths and the people "enjoy" their punishment. The land being desolate shall have the blessing of rest, and they having repented shall have the blessing of chastisement. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/26-34.html
- Trapp (labelled Calvinist on the page) reads "they shall accept" as: I will give them to do what I require of them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/lev-26.cfm

**v. 44:** Ellicott: a long exile is no proof that God has finally cast them off. https://biblehub.com/leviticus/26-44.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch link it to Romans 11:29: God does not take back His calling. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/26-44.htm
- Matthew Henry: God speaks as a tender Father that cannot find in his heart to disinherit a son that has been very provoking. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_026.cfm
- Clarke: God has kept the Jews as a distinct people through history. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/26-44.html

**v. 45:** The Pulpit Commentary says God brought them back after Babylon. In the same way, upon their repentance, he replaces in a state of salvation Churches and individuals that have fallen away from him. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/leviticus-26.html
- A Pulpit homily (Clarkson) applies this to Christians: God remembers his promise with us, sealed with a Saviour's blood. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/leviticus-26.html

**v. 46:** Matthew Henry: the law was made between God and Israel rather as a covenant than a law; for he draws with the cords of a man. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/26-44.html

---

## Where the commentators differ (vv. 40–45)

None of these sources says the disagreement follows denominational lines. These are differences I noticed between them.

- **Is the promise unconditional?**
  - Constable (Dr. Constable's Expository Notes; no tradition label on the page) calls these verses a strong witness to the unconditional nature of the Abrahamic Covenant. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/26-42.html
  - Precept Austin likewise says God will never reject Israel as a people group. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_26_commentary
  - Coffman (no tradition label on the page) disagrees: the promise is contingent, absolutely, upon their confession. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/26-44.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary leaves it open: Whether Jewish repentance has been or ever will be so full as to obtain this blessing, cannot be decided now. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/26-40.html
- **What fulfils the promise?**
  - Gill (labelled "Baptist · Calvinism" on the page) says Israel was cast off for rejecting the Messiah, but not destroyed. God will be gracious to them through Christ and for his sake, and convert and save them, see Romans 11:26.
  - Poole says Paul draws from passages like this that Israel should be gathered again and restored. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/26-44.htm
  - Chuck Smith reads it as "I will preserve them as an ethnic group," which God has done. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/26-40.html
  - Grant (studylight.org) connects the land promise to 1948. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/leviticus-26.html
- **What repentance involves (Methodist and Calvinist voices):**
  - The Methodist Joseph Benson (labelled "Arminian, Wesleyan/Methodist") says it means sincerely accepting God's correction and then obeying, which is a good evidence of true repentance. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/26-41.html
  - Precept Austin says an uncircumcised heart isn't a repentant heart, which implies God must circumcise their heart as described in Deuteronomy 30:6. https://www.preceptaustin.org/circumcision-of-the-heart
  - Trapp's note on v. 43 also stresses God's enabling (see above).

---

## Other views

- **Catholic translation:** the Douay-Rheims Bible puts v. 44 in the past tense: "I did not cast them off altogether". https://biblehub.com/leviticus/26-44.htm. It also leaves out "the land" in v. 42. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/hnv/leviticus/26-42.html. This is only a translation difference, not a Catholic commentary.
- **Ancient treaty background:** Guzik quotes Harrison and Rooker comparing the chapter to the blessing-and-curse endings of ancient Near Eastern treaties. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-26/
